nameStory: The tidewater mucket gets its name from its ability to live in the brackish waters where rivers meet the sea - the 'tidewater' zone where fresh and salt water mix. The word 'mucket' is an old American term for freshwater mussels, likely derived from the way these shellfish 'muck about' in river and stream bottoms.
description: The tidewater mucket is a freshwater mussel that looks like a smooth, elongated clam with a yellowish-brown shell. These bivalves spend their lives partially buried in sandy or muddy river bottoms, filtering water through their bodies to catch tiny food particles. They typically grow to about 2-4 inches long and have two hinged shell halves that can snap shut when disturbed. This species is quite special - it's the only member of its genus, making it a unique branch on the mussel family tree.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Elongated and oval-shaped, roughly twice as long as it is tall, with a smooth, streamlined appearance that feels almost polished when wet

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Yellowish-brown to tan exterior that may have subtle darker growth rings, while the interior is typically pearly white or pale yellow

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Relatively smooth surface with fine growth lines, lacking the heavy ridges or bumps found on many other mussel species

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in tidal freshwater areas where rivers approach the coast, tolerating slight saltiness that kills most other freshwater mussels

idTips.label: Burial pattern
idTips.description: Usually found with only the back edge of the shell visible above sand or mud, with two small tube-like openings for water intake and outflow

habitat: Look for tidewater muckets in the sandy or muddy bottoms of coastal rivers and streams, especially in areas where fresh water meets tidal influence. They prefer slow-moving waters with good sediment for burrowing, typically found from the water's edge down to about 6 feet deep. In New England, they're most likely in tidal reaches of rivers flowing into coastal bays and estuaries.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot them as water levels drop and warming temperatures make them more active in their feeding and filtering behaviors.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're filtering water rapidly; look for the telltale siphon openings in sandy bottoms during low tide periods.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but beginning to reduce activity as water temperatures cool; shells may be more obvious as vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Least active period when they remain buried deeply in sediment, making them very difficult to locate without careful searching.

funFact: This mussel can actually survive in slightly salty water that would kill most freshwater mussels, making it a living bridge between marine and freshwater worlds - like a shellfish that speaks two different chemical languages!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other elongated freshwater mussels like the Eastern elliptio, but the tidewater mucket's preference for brackish tidal areas and its smoother, more streamlined shell help distinguish it. Remember: if you find it where the river tastes slightly salty, you've probably found a tidewater mucket.
contextualKnowledge: Scientists recently moved this species from the old genus Leptodea into its own unique genus Atlanticoncha, recognizing that it's different enough from other mussels to deserve its own special category. This name change reflects our growing understanding of mussel diversity and evolution.
compareHints: As the sole member of its genus Atlanticoncha, the tidewater mucket stands alone among New England mussels in its tolerance for brackish water. Compared to other river mussels in the Unionidae family, it's more elongated and smooth-shelled than the chunky, ridged Eastern elliptio, and much smaller than the large washboard mussel. Its streamlined shape and coastal habitat make it fairly distinctive once you know what to look for.
